title.en: The Popol Wuj: Failed Creations, the Lords of Xibalba, and the Hero Twins
title.zh: 《波波爾·烏》：失敗的造人、希巴爾巴諸主與英雄雙子

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）

texts.period: Original text c. 1554-1578 (post-conquest, K'iche' language, original hieroglyphic or early alphabetic); surviving transcription by Francisco Ximenez c. 1701-03; MS: Ayer MS 1515, Newberry Library, Chicago

source.archive: Newberry Library (Ayer MS 1515) / Mesoweb (Christenson literal translation)
source.work: Popol Wuj, K'iche' text and trans. Allen J. Christenson (literal edition, 2003-04); Dennis Tedlock, Popol Vuh (rev. ed., 1996)

texts.license: English translations quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Heart of Sky and the Sovereign Plumed Serpent attempt the world four times — mud, wood, maize — until the Hero Twins descend to Xibalba, trick the lords of death into sacrificing and NOT reviving themselves, and rise as sun and moon; from ground maize the true people of corn are made, and the K'iche' lineages begin.
summary.zh: 創世者與羽蛇神四次造世——泥人、木人皆敗，終以玉米成真人；英雄雙子下希巴爾巴冥府，設計使死亡諸主自殺而不得復活，升為日月；以磨過之玉米造出今日之人類，基切族裔自茲而始。

sensitivity.note: Living K'iche' tradition; the Popol Wuj is treated by some Maya communities as sacred counsel. Only published scholarly translations are summarized; no restricted or unpublished ceremonial text is reproduced.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Part 1 (Tedlock pp. 63-75): The earth is raised from the water by the words of Tepeu and Gucumatz with Heart of Sky; the animals are made and given their homes, but they cannot speak the names of their makers — so their flesh is doomed to be caught and eaten. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Part 1 (Tedlock pp. 63-75); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Part 3: Hunahpu and Xbalanque, having beaten the lords of Xibalba at their own game of sacrifice, rise into the sky — one as the sun, one as the moon; the 400 boys who died with Zipacna become their stars. Then Xmucane grinds yellow and white maize nine times and washes it, and the water becomes human flesh. Not verbatim.

texts.language: Classical K'iche' (Mayan) written in Latin alphabet
texts.canonical_translation: Dennis Tedlock, Popol Vuh: The Mayan Book of the Dawn of Life, rev. ed., New York, 1996; Allen J. Christenson, Popol Vuh: Literal Poetic Version, 2003-04

narrative.en:
The Popol Wuj ('Book of the Council/Mat') opens by declaring itself 'the first book, written long ago', now hidden: the council-book of the K'iche' nation that survived the conquest — 'we shall bring it to light because the Popol Wuj is no longer to be seen'. Its three parts tell creation, the twins, and the founding of the K'iche' lineages.

PART ONE: THE FAILED CREATIONS. Before the world, there is only sea, a quiet expanse of sky, and the gods gathered in the darkness: the Framer and the Shaper, Sovereign and Quetzal Serpent, the Bearer and Begetter, and Heart of Sky (Hurricane, Chipi-Caculha, and Rattle-snake — the trinity of the lightning gods), who speak with Sovereign Plumed Serpent 'in the darkness, in the night' and conceive 'the ripening of the dawn': merely by words, earth rises from the water — mountains and valleys appear, and the forests bud. Then come the animals — deer and birds — each given its home and its way; but they cannot speak or praise their makers ('they only squawk, chatter, and howl'), so their flesh is condemned: 'you shall be caught and eaten'.

The gods try again: a human shape is made of mud, but it dissolves — it cannot move, it crumbles. A third attempt: effigies carved of wood. The wood people look human, speak, and multiply — 'but there was nothing in their hearts and nothing in their minds, no memory of their masons and builders'. They do not remember their makers, and the gods' gifts are wasted; Heart of Sky resolves to destroy them. A flood of black rain comes day and night; the dogs and turkeys, the grinding stones, the cooking pots, even their own hearthstones rise against them — the household implements they abused now bite them ('you have beaten us, now you shall feel our teeth'). Those who survive become the monkeys in the trees — and the text slyly notes that this is why monkeys 'look like the form of a person': a parody of humanity, not its ancestor.

Between creations comes the comic-serious episode of Vucub Caquix ('Seven Macaw'), a self-styled sun who pretends to be the dawn, his teeth of metal; the twin boys Hunahpu and Xbalanque, still boys, shoot him from his nance tree with a blowgun, and, posing as curers, tear out his metal teeth and eyes (he must content himself with maize kernels); his sons Zipacna (who claims to have made the mountains, and is buried in a crab's pit-trap that becomes the hill 'Split Earth') and Cabracan (who shakes mountains, killed by the poisoned bird lure Zaqico — mountains brought down on him) are likewise removed: the world is cleared of false suns before the true dawn can come.

PART TWO: THE HERO TWINS' FATHERS. Xmucane and Xpiyacoc, the divine grandparents, bear two sons, One Hunahpu and Seven Hunahpu, skilled in dice and in the ballgame. Their playing disturbs the lords of Xibalba ('the place of fear'), whose council — One Death and Seven Death at the head, with the lords of Pus Blood, Bone Scepter, Scrapings, Wing, Packstrap, Blood Teethe, and All Seizes You — summon them down the dark river-crossings and the bird's messengers (the salt-gourd tapirs of the crossing). The brothers pass the dark river and the river of pus, the crossroads, and the Council Hall; the lords' test — a torch and two cigars that must return undiminished and unburnt — is failed (the brothers burn them up); they are sacrificed and buried at the Place of Ballgame Sacrifice. One Hunahpu's severed head is hung in a calabash tree, which fruits; the maiden Ixquic ('Blood Maiden') comes to see, and the skull spits into her hand — 'this is just a sign', says the head, 'I have only given you my saliva' — and she conceives. Sentenced to death by her father One Batz, she escapes to Xmucane's house, proving her maternity by the miraculous filled basket of maize (she returns with one grain per tuft from the miraculous field).

PART THREE: THE TWINS. Xmucane bears the boys Hunahpu and Xbalanque; their elder half-brothers, the Howler Monkey Boys (flautists and singers, jealous of the newborns), are tricked out of their garden (the twins shoot birds and leave the garden-watching to them), and lured into trees where their belts become tails — they become monkeys, 'the patron of flute players and singers', and are welcomed as such, weeping (Xmucane grieves but the twins tell her not to mourn). The boys now clear the garden in a night by magic (the tools do the work while they sleep), and, betrayed by the tell-tale songs of the rabbits and rats, they hunt in turn: the rat is spared by promising to lead them to the grandfather's hidden ballgame gear, dug out of the house's center, where One Hunahpu's ballgame equipment had been buried.

The lords of Xibalba hear the ballgame's noise and summon the twins (as they summoned the fathers); the boys play briefly, excuse themselves, and set out for Xibalba to avenge their fathers. They cross the river of pus and the dark river on their blowguns, sending a fake mosquito (Xan) ahead to prick the sitting lords and learn their names (Hunahpu and Xbalanque greet each lord by name — 'this is how we distinguish them from mannequins'), then fail the test deliberately: the House of Gloom, the House of Knives (blades blunted by the deal — in some tellings by the twins' magic), the House of Cold, the House of Jaguars (fed bones), the House of Bats: Hunahpu peeks to see the dawn and is decapitated by Camazotz, lord of bats; Xbalanque substitutes a squash for his brother's head, and the rabbit decoys the pursuing lords into the ballgame court; the brothers win the game in which the head is again a squash, bursting it.

Now the twins grind the fathers' bones, scatter them in the river ('fine as corn meal'), and after five days of silence rise as catfish-people, then as boys of miracle: they dance, burn Xibalba's houses and dogs (and restore them), turn themselves into catfish and opossums, and finally perform in the lords' court: they sacrifice a dog and revive it, sacrifice themselves — Hunahpu kills Xbalanque and scatters him, then revives him. One Death and Seven Death demand the performance for themselves; the twins kill them — and do NOT revive them. The lords are dead; the boys reveal themselves by name, ascending into the sky: 'so they rose as the sun and the moon' (Tedlock's footnote notes local tellings differ: one is the sun, the other the moon or Venus), and the four hundred boys who died with Zipacna become their stars (the Pleiades in local commentary). The dawn comes at last to the true world.

PART FOUR: THE PEOPLE OF MAIZE. The grandmothers grind white and yellow maize nine times, wash the flour, and the water becomes human flesh; four men are made — Jaguar Quitze, Jaguar Night, Not Right Now, and Dark Jaguar — with four wives (Caha Paluma, Choimha, Tzununmo, Caquixa). They see perfectly, 'as soon as they looked they saw all', and give thanks — but the gods cloud their eyes ('it was not well that our first creatures should see everything') so they see only what is near, as people now do. The four men and their wives beget the K'iche' lineages; they receive their god-bundles at Tulan-Zuiva ('the seven caves, the seven canyons'), where the languages of the peoples are divided ('our speech is changed'), and they migrate — the text narrates the crossing of rivers, the sorrows of leaving the East, and the taking of Q'umarkaj, 'Rotten Cane', the K'iche' capital.

FUNCTIONS. The Popol Wuj is the charter of K'iche' polity and lineage legitimacy (each named ancestor grounds a real descent group), a theology of maize as human flesh, a cosmology of the ballgame and of death's defeat by trickery; post-conquest it preserved K'iche' historical memory in alphabetic K'iche', and it remains recited, taught, and performed (Tedlock's working translation was made with the K'iche' ritualist Andres Xiloj, 1975-76) — a living text as much as a colonial survivor.
narrative.zh: 序言自述為基切族之議事之書，證其源遠而存於征服之後。第一卷：造世者與羽蛇神偕心之中心（呼瑞堪、三雷神）於黑暗中言出大地；造獸而不諳其名，遂為食；泥人碎，木人無心，洪水黑雨滅之，倖存者化為猴。其間七金剛鸚鵡自稱太陽，雙子射齒拔眼誅之；其子斯巴坎那、卡布拉坎亦次第除滅。第二卷：烏與斯巴烏善賭戲，擾希巴爾巴諸主，被召入冥府，火把與雪茄之試不成而被誅；烏之首懸於葫蘆樹，吐唾於伊希魁之手而使之孕；伊希魁逃至祖母處，以奇蹟盈筐之玉米證明孕育。第三卷：雙子胡納普與斯巴蘭克生，先化兄為猴，再應召下冥府：渡膿河與暗河，遣假蚊問名，夜宿刀屋、寒屋、豹屋，蝙蝠屋中胡納普被卡馬索茲斬首，南瓜代首、兔誘追兵；後磨骨撒河，五日無聲，化魚而復生為神童：獻狗復活、自戕復活，諸主欲試，雙子殺之而不復活——死亡諸主遂滅。二人升天：一為日、一為月，四百童子為星。第四卷：祖母九磨黃白玉米，水為人肉；四男四女生基切諸族；於圖蘭分語言，遷徙至庫馬爾卡赫。功能：族裔合法性之憲章、玉米為肉之神學、球賽宇宙觀與以詭勝死之釋義。

Theology of maize: human flesh ground from corn, nine times
Ballgame cosmology; defeat of death by trickery and non-revival
Post-conquest survival text: alphabetic K'iche' memory, recited and taught today

variants.name: Francisco Ximenez transcription (Ayer MS 1515)
variants.summary: The unique surviving manuscript: Ximenez, a Dominican, transcribed a K'iche' original (now lost) with facing Spanish; all modern editions derive from this copy, with Scherzer 1857 and Brasseur de Bourbourg 1861 as first printings.

variants.name: Tedlock's performative translation (with Andres Xiloj)
variants.text_tradition: Fieldwork 1975-76 with the K'iche' daykeeper Andres Xiloj (Momostenango)
variants.summary: Tedlock's translation is built around Xiloj's live commentary on the divinatory and ritual meanings (day names, ballgame movements, the twins' calendar); the named collaborator is integral to the text's authority.

variants.name: Classic Maya ceramic parallels
variants.text_tradition: Polychrome vessels (Kerr Maya Vase Database, 8th-9th c. CE, lowland Maya)
variants.summary: Lowland polychrome pottery shows the Hero Twins' dance, the Lords of Death as skeletal performers, and the head-restoration scene — suggesting the highland narrative shares a deep Maya narrative pool with the lowland classic corpus.

variants.name: Contemporary K'iche' recitation
variants.text_tradition: K'iche' communities, highland Guatemala (e.g. Sam Colop's 1999 K'iche' edition)
variants.summary: Luis Enrique Sam Colop's K'iche'-language edition (1999) anchors the text as living literature rather than colonial archive; communities treat it variously as history, counsel, and sacred narrative.

title.en: Osiris, Isis, and Horus: Murder, Dismemberment, and the Contendings for the Throne
title.zh: 奧西里斯、伊西斯與荷魯斯：弒君分屍與王位之爭

region.en: Abydos, Upper Egypt (Osiris' principal cult center)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及阿拜多斯（奧西里斯主祭中心）

texts.period: Narrative assembled from Pyramid Texts (c. 2350-2175 BCE), Middle Kingdom ritual dramas, New Kingdom Papyrus Chester Beatty I (c. 1200-1150 BCE, BM EA 10688), and Plutarch's De Iside et Osiride (1st-2nd c. CE)

source.archive: British Museum (Papyrus Chester Beatty I) / Loeb Classical Library (Plutarch)
source.work: The Contendings of Horus and Seth (P. Chester Beatty I, trans. A. H. Gardiner, Late-Egyptian Stories, 1932); Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride, ed. J. Gwyn Griffiths, 1970

texts.license: Ancient texts public domain; modern editions quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Osiris, the good king, is murdered and dismembered by his brother Seth; Isis gathers the body, conceives Horus, and raises him in the marshes; before the divine tribunal Horus contends for eighty years — through contests, lettuce, a stone boat, and a letter from Osiris himself — until Horus is vindicated and Osiris becomes king and judge of the dead.
summary.zh: 善王奧西里斯遭弟塞特謀殺分屍；伊西斯尋屍合體，孕荷魯斯於沼澤撫育；神庭之爭歷八十年——變形角力、萵苣施術、石舟競渡、亡父親函——荷魯斯終得復仇之審，父王遂為冥府之王與審判者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary and funerary corpus; no living community restrictions. Modern Kemetic (reconstructionist) communities treat the material as heritage.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of The Contendings (P. Chester Beatty I, 5.5-6.10): The tribunal has sat for eighty years without deciding; Isis transforms herself and tricks Seth into self-condemnation ('a man's property should go to his widow's son'); Re is angry, and Seth proposes a contest — to become hippopotami and see who can stay three months under the sea. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of The Contendings (P. Chester Beatty I, 5.5-6.10); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the verdict (P. Chester Beatty I, 11.1-9): A letter comes from Osiris in the West — 'what good is it that I have been made, when no one stands in fear of me?' — and the Ennead, terrified of famine, finally rules: 'Horus, son of Isis, is to be given the office of his father Osiris.' Seth is led away in chains to be bound to Re's bark as the thunder's voice. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the verdict (P. Chester Beatty I, 11.1-9); not verbatim.

texts.language: Middle and Late Egyptian; Ancient Greek (Plutarch)
texts.canonical_translation: A. H. Gardiner, Late-Egyptian Stories (Bruxelles, 1932) for The Contendings; J. Gwyn Griffiths, Plutarch's De Iside et Osiride, Cardiff, 1970

narrative.en:
Egypt never preserved one canonical book of the myth; the narrative is assembled across a thousand years from funerary spells, temple liturgy, a satirical New Kingdom papyrus, and a Greek philosophical retelling.

BEGINNING: THE GOOD KING AND THE MURDER. Geb, the earth, divides the inheritance between his sons: Osiris receives Egypt, Seth the desert (so the New Kingdom 'Contendings' opens). Osiris, the first king, gives humanity agriculture, law, and cult, and governs with Isis, his sister-wife — the ideal rule. Seth, jealous, conspires (Plutarch, De Iside 13: with 72 conspirators and a queen of Ethiopia) : at a banquet Seth produces a beautifully wrought chest and promises it to whoever fits inside; when Osiris lies down, the lid is nailed shut, sealed with lead, and the chest is cast into the Nile at Tanis, borne out to sea. (In native sources, the murder's mechanism is alluded to more obliquely — the 'striking down of Osiris', with the Nile's flood as the season of his death.)

THE SEARCH AND THE DISMEMBERMENT. Isis, with her sister Nephthys, searches for the chest — the lament genre ('Come to thy house, come to thy house!') already fixed in the Pyramid Texts and elaborated in New Kingdom hymns. The chest lands at Byblos on the Phoenician coast, grown into the pillar of the king's palace; Isis serves as nurse to the royal child, healing him in the fire (like a Demeter), reveals herself, and takes the pillar. In the Delta marsh of Akh-biten she opens the chest — and Seth, hunting by moonlight, finds the body: he dismembers Osiris (Plutarch: fourteen pieces scattered through Egypt; Diodorus says twenty-six; the Egyptian texts simply speak of the body cut in pieces and the limbs gathered). Isis and Nephthys gather the limbs; where each piece was buried, a tomb claims him (aition of the many Osiris tombs); the phallus, thrown to the Nile, is eaten by fish (Plutarch's aition for the abstinence from fish), and Isis fashions a model phallus — the origin of the festival images. With winged arms and the breath of her magic, Isis revives Osiris just enough to conceive Horus ('the heir'), then the god withdraws to rule the West.

MIDDLE: THE CONTENDINGS. The child Horus, 'the fledgling in the nest of Chemmis', is raised in the Delta marshes; when grown, he claims his father's office. The Ennead (nine gods) convenes on the mountain to judge between Horus and Seth — 'for eighty years' the tribunal sits without decision, the Contendings notes satirically, with Re-Harakhti shouting that Horus is too young. The contest episodes: (1) Isis transforms herself into a beautiful maiden; Seth, smitten, tells her of his own claim ('I am the one who protects the bark of Re') — 'a man's property should go to his widow's son', she replies, and Seth condemns himself out of his own mouth. (2) The hippopotamus contest: each transforms into a hippopotamus to stay three months under the sea; Isis harpoons Seth even as he protects her son, and Horus, furious, cuts off his mother's head (Thoth restores it with a cow's head — aition of the Hathor-cow). (3) The boat race: cedar boats — Seth's lined with lead, Horus's of stone — and Seth's sinks. (4) The lettuce episode: Seth proposes the two contend as hippopotami again; Horus, urged by Isis, takes Seth's lettuce (prepared with Horus' semen by Isis' magic); when Seth boasts of 'doing a man's work' with Horus, Thoth summons the semen: it answers from Seth's forehead, is drawn out as a golden sun-disk from his crown, and Horus is vindicated as the seed-giver. (5) Osiris' letter: the tribunal still hesitates until a letter arrives from the West — 'what good is it that I have been made [in the Duat], when no one stands in fear of me?... This land is in my hand... the barley, the emmer... I will let them be taken to the sky' — the judges, terrified of famine, finally give judgment: 'Horus, son of Isis, is to be given the office of his father Osiris.' Shu and Thoth crown Horus; Seth is bound and brought before Re, who sets him at his bark to thunder in the sky ('you shall be my son, dwelling in the sky, my voice of thunder') — the moral ambiguity typical of the Egyptian telling.

END: OSIRIS KING OF THE DEAD. Osiris, in joy ('my heart flourishes, my house is avenged'), accepts the West: he becomes king and judge of the Duat, enthroned with Isis and Nephthys and the four Sons of Horus; every dead Egyptian, mummified like him, is called 'an Osiris'. Before him (Book of the Dead 125) the heart is weighed against Ma'at's feather before forty-two judges, with the negative confession ('I have not stolen... I have not killed... I have not made crooked the scale'), the Devourer (Ammit) waiting for the unjust. At Abydos (Middle Kingdom Ikhernofret Stela) his annual Mystery Procession re-enacted his death, battle, and triumphal return in the fields — with barley-bed 'Osiris gardens' germinating in coffin-shaped beds, the grain-god's resurrection image found throughout the land.

FUNCTIONS. The cycle is the charter of Egyptian kingship: every living king is 'the Horus', every dead one 'the Osiris' — the political theology Frankfort traced in Kingship and the Gods; it grounds mummification, the Book of the Dead 125 judgment, the Abydos pilgrimage and Khoiak mysteries, and the agricultural resurrection image of germinating grain; its lament genre (Isis and Nephthys) is the core Egyptian funerary performance.
narrative.zh: 地神蓋布分封二子：奧西里斯得埃及、塞特得荒漠。善王治世有法，弟嫉之，宴會造箱，誘其臥而釘蓋鉛封，投之尼羅河。伊西斯與妹妹尼弗提斯遍尋，箱至畢布勒斯化為王宮棟梁，伊西斯化身乳母取之；於三角洲沼澤啟箱，塞特獵月下遇屍，肢解而散置全境（普魯塔克：十四塊）。二女神集遺骸，各葬處即為其墓；陽具為魚所食，伊西斯以塑形代之；展翼施術，喚魂使孕，得荷魯斯。荷魯斯長成索父位，神庭議八十年不決：伊西斯化美女誘塞特自認其罪；化河馬之試、萵苣施術（塞特自誇而精液自額間呼出，證荷魯斯為種子之主）、石舟競渡；末得亡父自冥府來函：『此田在我手中……無人畏我，何益？』諸神懼饑饉乃決：『荷魯斯，伊西斯之子，承其父奧西里斯之位。』塞特被縛於拉神之舟為雷聲。奧西里斯心喜，遂王西方：為冥府之王與審判者；凡亡者皆稱『奧西里斯』，心臟於瑪特羽毛之前稱量，阿米特伺其不義。阿拜多斯年年演其死與復活之奧秘，穀倉棺形床中發芽，即穀神重生之像。功能：王權神學之憲章、木乃伊與稱心儀式之根、阿拜多斯朝聖與克霍伊亞克奧秘。

functions: Political theology of kingship: living king = Horus, dead king = Osiris
Foundation of funerary practice: mummification, Book of the Dead 125, the weighing of the heart
Abydos pilgrimage and Khoiak mysteries; grain-god resurrection imagery (Osiris gardens)
Lament genre of Isis and Nephthys as the core Egyptian funerary performance

variants.name: Pyramid Texts (Old Kingdom allusions)
variants.text_tradition: Pyramid Texts of Unas and later 5th-6th dynasty pyramids, c. 2350-2175 BCE
variants.summary: Scattered spells assume the story (the sky reddens at Osiris' death; Isis seeks; Horus avenges) without narrating it — evidence that the plot predates our earliest continuous texts; the dismemberment is alluded to in Utterance 357 and others.

variants.name: The Contendings of Horus and Seth (New Kingdom satire)
variants.text_tradition: Papyrus Chester Beatty I (BM EA 10688), c. 1200-1150 BCE
variants.summary: The fullest native narrative, told as court satire: the gods' bickering, Re's irritability, Hathor's flashing, the lettuce trick, and Osiris' threatening letter — the tone is comic, the verdict theological.

variants.name: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek allegory)
variants.text_tradition: Moralia 351C-384C, 1st-2nd c. CE; principal MSS: Parisinus, etc.
variants.summary: Provides the fixed numbers (72 conspirators, 14 pieces, the Byblos pillar, the fish-eaten phallus) and an Isis-Osiris-Horus triad read philosophically (Osiris = source and reason, Isis = receptive, Horus = the world); the standard classical source, filtered through Middle Platonism.

variants.name: Diodorus Siculus' Egyptian history
variants.summary: Gives 26 pieces (rather than 14) and a Dionysus-Osiris identification, illustrating how the myth's numbers varied in classical transmission.

variants.name: Ikhernofret Stela (Middle Kingdom ritual drama)
variants.text_tradition: Stela of Ikhernofret (Berlin 1204), reign of Sesostris III, c. 1870 BCE
variants.summary: An Abydos official describes the Khoiak Mystery Procession he staged: the Great Procession of Osiris, the 'Striking of the Enemy' (reenacted combat), the Night of Mystery (death and revival), and the return to the temple — the ritual narrative as performance.

title.en: Obatala, Oduduwa, and the Creation of Ile-Ife
title.zh: 奧巴塔拉、奧杜杜瓦與伊費創世

region.zh: 尼日利亞奧孫州伊雷-伊費

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded ethnographically c. 1938 onward (Bascom field recordings); Ifa odu corpus transmitted orally for centuries (UNESCO Intangible Heritage 2008)

source.archive: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication between Gods and Men in West Africa (Bloomington, 1969)
source.work: Ile-Ife creation narratives (Obatala/Oduduwa traditions) recorded by William Bascom and Yoruba scholars; Wande Abimbola, Ifa: An Exposition of Ifa Literary Corpus (Ibadan, 1976)

texts.license: Paraphrase summaries only; underlying oral texts are community heritage and are not reproduced verbatim

summary.en: Olodumare sends Obatala down from heaven on a chain with sand, a hen, and a palm kernel; drunk on palm wine, he sleeps, and Oduduwa completes the work, pouring the sand that becomes Ile-Ife — 'where the day broke' — the navel of the Yoruba world and the origin of its kings; Obatala is given the molding of human bodies from clay.
summary.zh: 至高神奧洛杜馬雷遣奧巴塔拉沿鐵鍊降世，攜沙、雞與棕櫚仁；奧巴塔拉因棕櫚酒醉眠，奧杜杜瓦代之傾沙成陸，成為伊費——『破曉之地』、約魯巴世界之臍與諸王之源；奧巴塔拉則受命以土塑人身。

sensitivity.note: Not excluded: this record contains paraphrase summaries only, built from published scholarship (Bascom 1969; Abimbola 1976). Some Ifa odu verses and royal Ife narratives ARE initiate-restricted and are not reproduced; see sensitivity_guidance and sensitivity_flag (living_tradition_high).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Ife tradition as published by Bascom (1969) and Abimbola (1976): Olodumare, the supreme being, sends Obatala from heaven on a chain, carrying a snail-shell of loose earth, a five-toed hen, and a palm kernel; Obatala first consults Ifa (the odu prescribed the offerings), pours the earth on the primordial waters, and the hen scratches it outward until land spreads — where the spread stops, hills rise; he plants the palm kernel and names the place Ife. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Ife tradition as published by Bascom (1969) and Abimbola (1976); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Obatala/Oduduwa episode as published by Bascom (1969): Obatala, on arriving, drinks palm wine (breaking his taboo for the mission) and sleeps; Oduduwa takes the materials and completes the pouring and spreading; the brothers dispute precedence, and Olodumare assigns Obatala the molding of human bodies from clay — whose imperfect forms (hunchbacks, cripples) explain human difference and Obatala's protective care for the deformed. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Obatala/Oduduwa episode as published by Bascom (1969); not verbatim.

texts.language: Yoruba (oral, tonal; Ifa chants in recitative style)
texts.canonical_translation: Published scholarly paraphrases (Bascom 1969; Abimbola 1976); no canonical written text exists — the tradition is oral and variant

narrative.en:
The Ife creation narrative is not a single text but a family of oral traditions, recited in Ifa divination verses (odu) and in royal praise-poetry, with regional and political variants. The summary below follows the published scholarly paraphrases and flags the contested points.

BEGINNING: THE DESCENT. In the beginning there is only sky (orun) and the watery waste (aye) below, over which Olodumare (Olorun, the owner/sky-being) rules. Olodumare determines to create solid land and chooses Obatala, the first orisha of the royal line, to do it: first, Obatala must consult Ifa, the divination system of Orunmila, whose odu prescribe the offerings (the divination myth itself is thereby the charter of Ifa's primacy). Obatala descends from heaven on a long chain, carrying a snail-shell of loose earth, a five-toed hen, and a palm kernel. Arriving over the waters, he pours the earth into a heap; the hen scratches and scatters it outward in every direction until it forms land — where the spreading stopped, hills remain (the aition of Ife's topography). Obatala plants the palm kernel (from which the palm tree grows, source of wine, oil, and many uses) and names the place Ile-Ife — 'the house of spreading' or, in the common gloss, 'the place where the day broke' (ibere aye), the spot where the world's light first shone.

MIDDLE: THE DRUNKEN SLEEP AND ODUDUWA. Obatala, having accomplished the work, drinks palm wine — in some tellings to celebrate, in others seduced by the tree he planted — and breaks the taboo of his mission. He sleeps. Oduduwa (in Ife tradition a brother or fellow-divine agent; in Oyo royal tradition, the ancestor-sultan who completed creation) takes the snail-shell and the hen, completes the pouring, and claims the work: 'I have created the earth.' On waking, Obatala is humiliated; the brothers dispute precedence, and Olodumare intervenes: Oduduwa's act stands — the earth is his — and the earth's kingship descends through him (the Ooni of Ife and, in Oyo versions, the Alaafin claim descent); Obatala is consoled with a different office: the molding of human bodies.

END: THE MOLDING OF HUMANKIND. Obatala, at the hill of Ife (in some tellings at a house of clay), molds human figures from earth — each one different, some hunchbacked, some crippled, some blind — and Olodumare breathes life into them. The deformed bodies are Obatala's work and therefore under his protection: the tradition aitiologizes both human difference and the Orisha's care for the disabled, and grounds Obatala's cult taboos (no palm wine; white cloth, purity, coolness — Obatala is the orisha of white chalk, of calm heads and clear judgment). Ile-Ife remains the sacred origin-point: 'Ife is where the work of creation was done' — the origin of humanity and the source from which kingship radiated to the Yoruba kingdoms (Oyo, Benin's dynasty in some tellings, Ketu, Sabe) — and the Ooni of Ife is acknowledged as spiritual head of the Yoruba world.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative is the charter of Yoruba kingship (the Ife-centered royal genealogies), of Ifa's divinatory primacy (the odu consulted before the descent), of Obatala's cult (white cloth, palm-wine taboo, care for the deformed), and of Ile-Ife's sacred geography (topography aitiologized; the Ooni's primacy). It is also the ground on which 19th-20th century 'Yoruba' identity was built — the ethnonym itself is a modern back-formation, and the narrative's political variants map real inter-kingdom rivalries (Ife vs. Oyo vs. Benin).
narrative.zh: 太初唯有天界與下方水域。奧洛杜馬雷遣奧巴塔拉沿鐵鍊降世，先諮詢伊法占卜（奧杜經文定祭品）：攜蝸牛殼之沙、五趾雞與棕櫚仁；傾沙於水，雞抓而四散，陸地遂成，丘留於散處；植棕櫚仁，名其地伊費——『破曉之地』。奧巴塔拉因棕櫚酒破戒而眠；奧杜杜瓦代之傾沙、完成造陸，兄弟爭先，奧洛杜馬雷裁定：地歸奧杜杜瓦，王權沿其後裔（伊費之奧尼、奧約之阿拉芬皆有宣稱）；奧巴塔拉受命以土塑人，形體或有殘缺，皆其所造而受其護佑——釋人類之異與其白布、禁酒、護殘之祭儀。伊費遂為神聖起源之地與約魯巴王權之放射中心。功能：王權憲章、伊法占卜至上之證、奧巴塔拉祭儀之根、伊費地理之釋義。

functions: Charter of Yoruba kingship: Ife as origin-point and the Ooni's spiritual primacy
Ifa divination's primacy: the odu consulted before creation itself
Obatala's cult: white cloth, palm-wine taboo, and care for the deformed
Ethnogenesis: the narrative's political variants map Ife-Oyo-Benin rivalries

variants.name: Ife version (Obatala first, Oduduwa completes)
variants.text_tradition: Ile-Ife royal and Ifa tradition (recorded Bascom 1969; Abimbola 1976)
variants.summary: Obatala descends, drinks, and sleeps; Oduduwa completes the work and is given the earth; Obatala is given the molding of humans. The Ooni of Ife is the world's spiritual head.

variants.name: Oyo version (Oduduwa as founder-ancestor)
variants.text_tradition: Alaafin's court traditions (recorded in Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, 1921, from 19th c. Oyo accounts)
variants.summary: Oduduwa is the first king of Ife and father of the dynasties; Obatala's role is reduced or omitted — the Oyo imperial claim to legitimacy, politically motivated against Ife's primacy.

variants.name: Benin version (Eweka line)
variants.text_tradition: Benin royal tradition (recorded in Jacob Egharevba, A Short History of Benin, 1934)
variants.summary: Oduduwa's son Oranmiyan (Eweka) founds the Benin dynasty — the story radiates Ife's kingship outward and grounds Benin's own legitimacy claims.

variants.name: Ifa odu recitations (Oduduwa/Obatala in divination verses)
variants.text_tradition: Ifa corpus (256 odu, oral, sung); Bascom 1969 records verses with named informants and odù names
variants.summary: The creation narrative appears inside divination verses as the moral-mythic warrant for divination's fees and sacrifices — the same story functions as ritual charter rather than origin-tale; some odu are initiate-restricted and not published.

title.en: Maui of Aotearoa: The Snared Sun, the Fished Island, and Hine-nui-te-po
title.zh: 毛利之毛伊：縛日、釣島與夜之女神

region.en: Te Ika-a-Maui (North Island), Aotearoa New Zealand

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in Sir George Grey's Polynesian Mythology (Auckland, 1855) from named Te Arawa informants incl. Wiremu Maihi Te Rangikaheke

source.archive: NZETC (Victoria University of Wellington) / Internet Archive (Grey 1855)
source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race (Auckland, 1855); Margaret Orbell, The Illustrated Encyclopedia of Maori Myth and Legend (Christchurch, 1995)

texts.license: Grey 1855 public domain; Orbell 1995 quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Maui-tikitiki-a-Taranga, last-born and mocked, snares the sun with ropes to slow its race; fishes up the North Island with a hook of ancestral jawbone and his own blood; steals fire's secret from Mahuika; and finally, seeking immortality, enters the sleeping giantess of death, Hine-nui-te-po — the birds laugh, she wakes, and death remains in the world.
summary.zh: 幼子毛伊遭兄嘲弄，以繩縛日使其慢行；以祖顎骨之鉤、自血為餌，釣起北島；自火神瑪胡伊卡處竊得火種之秘；末欲求不死，潛入睡臥之死亡巨女希紐伊特波——雀鳥輕笑，巨女驚醒，人類自此有死。

sensitivity.note: Living Maori tradition (matauranga Maori). Grey 1855 is a colonial-era collection of named Te Arawa informants, published with attribution; contemporary iwi and Maori scholarship (Orbell) is prioritized. Some narratives are tapu in context; only published paraphrases are reproduced.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Grey (1855), 'Maui and the Sun': Maui says to his brothers: 'Let us snare the sun, that he may not travel so fast'; they twist ropes of flax, and when the sun rises from his pit, Maui beats him with the enchanted jawbone of Murirangawhenua until he promises to go slowly — hence the long days of summer. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Grey (1855), 'Maui and the Sun'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Grey (1855), 'Maui and Hine-nui-te-po': Maui says: 'Let us seek death or life; if she sleeps, I will enter her body and pass through it, and death shall have no power.' The little birds (tiwaiwaka, fantail) laugh at his approach and wake her; the thighs close, and Maui is killed — hence death came into the world, and no man has escaped it since. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Grey (1855), 'Maui and Hine-nui-te-po'; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, 1855 (public domain); Margaret Orbell, Maori Myth and Legend, 1995 (modern Maori-authored synthesis)

narrative.en:
The Maori Maui cycle is the best-documented Polynesian variant of a figure known across the Pacific (Hawaiian, Samoan, Tongan, Tahitian). The fullest early record is Sir George Grey's Polynesian Mythology (1855), assembled from named Te Arawa informants, above all Wiremu Maihi Te Rangikaheke — a relatively well-provenanced colonial collection, flagged as such.

BEGINNING: THE LAST-BORN. Taranga, mother of five, casts her last-born into the sea at birth wrapped in a knot of her hair (topknot); the sea-ancestor Tama-nui-ki-te-Rangi finds and raises him. When Maui comes to his mother's village he finds four older brothers who mock the newcomer; his mother sends him to them as 'Maui-tikitiki-a-Taranga' ('Maui of the topknot of Taranga'), and the brothers, grudging, take him fishing — where he outperforms them all, and reveals his powers of transformation (he turns into birds, dogs, fish at will).

THE SNARING OF THE SUN. The days are too short: the sun (Te Ra) races across the sky so fast that food cannot be cooked and work cannot be done. Maui says to his brothers: 'Let us snare the sun, that he may go more slowly.' They twist great ropes of flax (the source says of the white-flowered flax) and noose them into nets; they build a fortress of clay (to hide behind), and at dawn, when the sun rises from his pit, Maui rises in his enchanted jawbone (the jawbone of his ancestor Murirangawhenua, which he has taken without leave) and beats the sun's face until the sun cries out — 'you will kill me!' — and promises to go slowly: 'hence the long days of summer'.

THE FISHING UP OF TE IKA. Maui tells his brothers to sail far out to sea ('do not look back, do not speak of your own doings'); he strikes his nose and smears his blood (his own sacred blood, tapu) on the jawbone-hook; he baits it and casts. The hook catches on the house of Tonganui, the great fish under the sea — and Maui hauls up the North Island, Te Ika-a-Maui ('the fish of Maui'), while his brothers, disobeying, carve at the catch with their adzes (greedy for food), cutting the valleys and ridges into the land. The South Island is Maui's canoe (Te Waka-a-Maui), and Stewart Island its anchor-stone — the entire cartography of Aotearoa hangs on this narrative. (In some tellings the giant fish is Tonganui, the grandson of Tangaroa, god of the sea.)

THE FIRE QUEST. Maui puts out all the fires of his village (in punishment for a slight, or by accident while the family are out); his mother sends him to Mahuika, the fire-goddess, ancestress of fire. He pretends his fires went out by chance; Mahuika, generous, plucks one of her fingernails (each finger a flame) and gives it; Maui, trickster, returns again and again with excuses ('the wind blew it out') until Mahuika, furious, throws her last fingernail at him — the world catches fire; Maui transforms himself into a hawk and flees (the land scorches behind him: Grey notes the burnt country of the story), and calls on his ancestors — Rangi the sky sends floods of rain, and the sea (Tangaroa) puts out the fire, while Maui turns himself into a mu (a bird) or (in some tellings) into a kaka hawk. All fire is extinguished except what Mahuika's flames had hidden in the kaikomako and tōtara trees — whence Maui teaches humanity to kindle fire by friction (hika: the fire-drill, kaikomako wood), the aition of Polynesian fire-making.

END: HINE-NUI-TE-PO. Maui has made the sun slow, the islands fished, fire kindled — the last enemy is death itself. He sees Hine-nui-te-po ('Great Woman of Night'), the giantess who guards the passage of the dead (her eyes are greenstone, her hair kelp, her mouth a shark's jaws); Maui says to the birds with him: 'If she sleeps I will enter her body, pass through it, and come out by her mouth — then death will not hold men, and mankind will be immortal.' The little tiwaiwaka (fantail) — in some tellings the riroriro (grey warbler) — laughs at the sight, and Hine-nui-te-po wakes and crushes Maui between her thighs; he dies, the first man to die by the great night. 'Hence', Grey's text concludes, 'death came into the world, and no man has escaped it since.' The culture-hero who defeated every obstacle is defeated by death — the aition of human mortality.

FUNCTIONS. The cycle aitiologizes Aotearoa's geography (Te Ika-a-Maui, Te Waka-a-Maui), the sun's pace, fire-by-friction, and human mortality; Maui-tikitiki is the trickster-culture-hero whose transformations teach that form is negotiable; the narratives are taught on the marae, in kapa haka, and in kōhanga reo as part of matauranga Maori, and the figure's name is claimed for canoes, landmarks, and institutions (e.g. 'Maui's dolphin').
narrative.zh: 毛伊乃塔蘭加之幼子，生而棄海，為祖先塔瑪努伊基特蘭吉所育；歸家為兄所嘲。初縛日：以亞麻繩結網，黎明時伏於土壘，持祖顎骨之力棒擊日面，日求饒而許緩行——夏日遂長。次釣島：以自血祭祖顎骨之鉤，深入遠洋，釣起北島『毛伊之魚』；兄違命以斧削之，遂成山谷；南島為其舟、斯圖爾特島為其錨石。再竊火：毛伊滅村中火，母遣其赴火神瑪胡伊卡；屢以藉口索火，神怒擲最後指甲，大地焚燒；毛伊化鷹而遁，祖先遣雨滅火；火種藏於卡伊科馬科與圖塔拉木中，毛伊遂教人鑽木取火。末求不死：見死亡巨女希紐伊特波，欲入睡臥之軀而穿過，令死亡失其權；雀鳥輕笑而驚醒巨女，巨女合股夾斃之——『死亡自茲入世，無人得免』。功能：新西蘭地理之釋義、日行之序、取火之由、人類有死之解；毛伊為毛利知識體系中之詭計英雄。

functions: Aitia of Aotearoa's geography: Te Ika-a-Maui, Te Waka-a-Maui, Stewart Island's anchor-stone
Aitia of the sun's pace and of fire-by-friction (kaikomako and tōtara trees)
Explanation of human mortality: the hero who defeated everything defeated by death
Living matauranga Maori: taught on marae, in kapa haka and kōhanga reo

variants.name: Hawaiian Maui
variants.text_tradition: Hawaiian oral tradition (recorded in 19th-20th c. collections, e.g. Fornander, Nathaniel Emerson)
variants.summary: Hina is the mother; Maui snares the sun at Haleakala to lengthen the day for Hina's kapa-making; steals the secret of fire from the 'alae hen; fishes up islands with a magic hook; dies in a failed quest for immortality. Separate record planned.

variants.name: Samoan Ti'iti'i (Maui-Ti'iti'i)
variants.text_tradition: Samoan oral tradition (recorded in Fraser, Pratt collections, 19th c.)
variants.summary: Ti'iti'i tricks the earthquake-god Mafuie's fire, breaking one of his arms — fire belongs to humankind thereafter; variants give him the fishing-up of islands and the slowing of the sun. Separate record planned.

variants.name: Tongan Maui Kisikisi
variants.text_tradition: Tongan oral tradition (recorded in Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, 1924)
variants.summary: Maui Kisikisi fishes up the islands (Tonga as the fish), snares the sun with a noose of ropes, and seeks immortality from Hikule'o — the Tongan chain of the same Polynesian cycle.

variants.name: Tahitian and Tuamotuan Maui
variants.text_tradition: Tahitian/Tuamotuan oral tradition (recorded in Henry, Ancient Tahiti, 1928; Stimson, 1930s)
variants.summary: Maui-taha and related forms fish up islands and capture the sun; the Tuamotuan corpus preserves genealogical Maui poems tying the hero to deep Polynesian whakapapa traditions.
